views.description: Earth from 20,000 km at about 64 degrees phase: the Blue Marble base on Cesium's globe and on celestiary's sphere, both under celestiary's Bruneton pass

The Moon from 5,000 km at quarter phase: ion's LRO WAC tiles, lit by celestiary's Sun, against celestiary's texture.  The metered exposure lifts this frame 1.22× (its brightest 2% is 0.49 of a sunlit white; #86's PR B), both renders alike, and the terminator profile's absolute differences with it: 24/6.5 became 25/6.9, so the bounds are 30/8
Mars from 12,000 km at about 65 degrees phase: ion's Cesium Mars tiles under celestiary's atmosphere pass, against celestiary's texture

Earth from 4,000 km at night over Europe, the Sun behind the planet: the city lights, NASA's Black Marble, on Cesium's globe (GIBS tiles, drawn in a pass of their own) and on celestiary's sphere (its night texture), under celestiary's atmosphere pass, at the exposure the meter picks for the dark frame.  Before #93 the Cesium side was black (ratio 0.00).  The region is the lit land (pixels of 6 or more, of 255): the ocean floor's few levels are quantisation noise

Earth from 400 km over Italy, straight down at dusk with the Sun 16 degrees under the horizon: the lights through celestiary's atmosphere pass.  From this low, GIBS's 600 m tiles are sharp where celestiary's 11 km texture is a blur, so the median ratio of pixels (0.69) isn't the measure: the region's mean is, over every pixel.  Red read 0.89 to 0.95 over runs (the tiles' level settles differently), so 0.85
Earth from 400 km, straight down with the Sun about 14 degrees up (76 degrees phase): the low-sun haze over the ground, and the terminator's soft edge

Earth from 7.5 km over the Ganges plain, looking east with the Sun 8 degrees up: the day ground through celestiary's atmosphere pass, on both sides.  The eye-adaptation boost once hid it under the haze on both, alike, so the view also bounds each render's own luma

Earth from 6.5 km near Everest, looking up a valley at a ridge rising above celestiary's sphere's horizon: Cesium's terrain there has no counterpart in celestiary, so the ridge (the region) is checked against the ground below it (the reference) in Cesium's render, not against celestiary's, which has sky there.  Without the terrain's distance the atmosphere pass took the ridge for sky and drew the sky over it

Mars from 232 m in Valles Marineris, the Sun low on the left: Cesium's terrain lies mostly below Mars's datum, under celestiary's sphere.  Before #141's Mars fix the ground sphere's depth covered the terrain, the band between the terrain's horizon and the sphere's read as ground with the stars through it (mars-low-horizon-band), and terrain above the sphere's horizon was drawn as sky.  Over the ground, on against off: the table's haze to the sphere on both sides

The same view, the band on the right between Cesium's terrain's horizon and the sphere's, against the sky above it in Cesium's render.  Before #141's Mars fix it read as ground, with the stars through it (luma 0.48 of the sky's, blue/red 0.90); now the horizon's haze over far terrain

Mars from 4.4 km, a near ridge on the right crossing the sphere's horizon line, the far horizon on the left.  Before the surface's segment was marched, the pass cut the table's in-scatter and depth at the ridge, sky rays above that line and ground rays below, and a seam ran through the near ridge as if the far horizon showed through it: the rows on the line (the region) against the ridge just below (the reference), in Cesium's render

Mars from 658 m under its datum in Valles Marineris (the floor is 4.7 km under it), looking away from the Sun: the band between Cesium's terrain's horizon and the horizontal (the region) against the sky above it (the reference), in Cesium's render.  The eye is below the ground sphere, so the pass marches each ray to where it leaves the sphere and takes the tables from there; the band is the horizon's haze, on the sky side of the tables by construction.  With the eye lifted to the sphere and the band's rays clamped to its horizon, the side was float32 rounding, and on a real GPU the band was black (the user's 'flickering horizon')

The same spot, facing the Sun: the band on the right between the terrain's horizon and the horizontal (the region) against the bright sky above it (the reference), in Cesium's render.  Here the band read black under a white sky on the user's GPU; it is the horizon's haze, continuous with the sky above and the hazed terrain below

Earth from 16 m under its datum at the Dead Sea (the shore is 395 m under it in Cesium's terrain), looking north: the band between the far shore's horizon and the horizontal (the region, a few rows) against the sky just above it (the reference), in Cesium's render.  The user saw a black wedge there; it is the horizon's haze, as on Mars

Mars from 6 m, facing the Sun, with mountains 150-280 km off on the horizon: past the terrain distance's encodable range (5.5 D, 220 km from the ground).  The region is where their fragments stood in the first cut, which gave such pixels the ground sphere's depth, 170 m off from 6 m up, so they came out dark and near with dithered edges; the reference is the sky above.  They are a surface at least 5.5 D away, hazed into the horizon like the sky

Mars's day sky from Valles Marineris looking up, the Sun 18 degrees up and behind the camera: the zenith (the region, the top of the frame) against the sky 35 degrees lower (the reference, the bottom): the sky's gradient and its tan colour (blue/red under 1).  Before multiple scattering and the dust's published properties the zenith was 0.04 of a sunlit white surface and black on screen

The same spot, looking away from the Sun: the sky just over the anti-solar horizon (the region) against the sky 30 degrees up (the reference).  Single scattering through the dust's forward lobe left this sky nearly black; multiply scattered light fills it, a little brighter at the horizon than above

The same spot, facing the Sun: the aureole within 10 degrees of the Sun (the region) against the sky 40 degrees from it (the reference): brighter, and bluer (the dust scatters blue more sharply forward: blue/red 1.5 against 0.8), where the sky used to be white across the frame

Earth from 3 km over the outback at civil twilight (the Sun 5 degrees under the horizon), looking toward the sunset glow, landed (the L in s=, so the camera quaternion is in the landed frame): the metered exposure lifts the frame about 7× over the keyed exposure (#86's PR B), and Cesium's terrain must follow it, as the decode is scaled by the exposure over Earth's keyed one.  The sky band above the horizon on against off (the ground under it is two models at night: Cesium's night floor against an unlit sphere), and its luma, which a frame left at the keyed exposure would fail (about 8; it reads 115 with Cesium's terrain in the frame).  Parity waits for the exposure to settle before its two renders
